content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper applies an empirical experiment showing that models that consider the network structure for transduction predictive links are not able to predict inductive links. Then, for the inductive problem, a node sampling approach is proposed to create the datasets (reducing the number of edges that are eliminated), and for the classification process, an MLP with a node embedding approach is proposed (obtaining better results than state of the art transduction predictive link models).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well written and the differences among transductive, semi-inductive, and inductive are well explained. 

The related work can be improved. The end of this section mentions that has inspired many state-of-the-art inductive link prediction methods, but those are not cited or described. 

The limitation of the transductive model prediction is empirically demonstrated. However, a better value in Hits@Top 20 does not means that the other model is better. As a suggestion, you could analyze the curve for different values of K and figure out the change of this metric, maybe with K=19 the baseline performance drops to 0.89.

Even though the node sampling approach is not novel, the results are interesting. As a suggestion, study the theoretical advantages of this type of sampling instead of edge sampling for this type of problem. It will make your paper stronger. 

The results of subsection 5.3 are expected. The use of k-means is related to a good Davies-Bouldin score. So, it is not clear the idea of this subsection. Moreover, better embedding should be related to better classification. 

However, the main weakness of the paper is its novelty. The main idea is that the use of node embeddings without relational structures will improve the link prediction between nodes that do not have any relational structure. This is actually well-known and the first baselines models consider this type of approach. So, it is not surprising that models that do not consider relational structure will do better for inductive prediction in comparison to models based on relational structure.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clear, except for subsection 5.3. It is not clear the idea of this study. If you want to use the shuffled and random as baselines, it is not necessary to apply that study. 

The quality can be improved, please see the comments for strengths and weaknesses.

Besides the empirical demonstration that transduction predictive link models are not good for inductive predictive link, there is no novelty in the paper. The first baselines for link prediction were based on node attributes. So, it is not surprising that models that use relation information for link prediction will perform poorly if no relational information is given. 

Reproducibility must be improved. Most of the details are omitted. For example, what are the characteristics of the MLP used in the paper? It is impossible to figure out if models are actually overfitted or if the process was correct.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper lacks off novelty, and theoretical demonstrations. The idea could be publishable but more technical details must be incorporated. Most of the empirical demonstrations are already known by the community.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to the reviewer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We will incorporate them in the revised write-up of this work.

Adding our responses below:

[Reviewer] Weakness 1

[Response] We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We will add citations for two of the best-performing models in inductive link prediction on ILPC 2022 benchmark namely CascadER and Inductive NodePiece.  

[Reviewer] Weakness 2

[Response] We have used the benchmark performance metric proposed by OGB. We also report the AUROC and AUPRC values as they are widely used in the machine learning community. 

[Reviewer] Weakness 3

[Response] We will incorporate the theoretical advantages in the revised write-up of this work.

[Reviewer] Weakness 4

[Response] This is related to identifying community structures in networks. The nodes in a graph can be clustered using the connectivity information (graph topology) and/or the node attributes. Since we have shown that the graph topology cannot be exploited by the machine learning models in inductive link predictions, the ability of the node attributes in clustering similar nodes (in terms of the node attributes) is a measure of the information contained in the attributes. We show that pre-trained node attributes produce the best clustering of the nodes, hence they contain the most information beyond the graph topology and are the most suitable for inductive tests.  

[Reviewer] Weakness 5

[Response] It is indeed well-known to the community that the relational structure (graph topology) and the node attributes (independent of the relational data) combined drive the link prediction task. First, we show that the transductive link prediction is driven by only the relational structure and simple algorithms like the configuration model achieve performance comparable to the state-of-the-art neural network network-based approaches. Thus, the node attributes which are independent of the relation structure play a major role in inductive link prediction, although naively handpicked node attributes share redundant information with the topological features. Furthermore, we develop a method for selecting the best-suited node attributes. We quantify the information contained in the node attributes beyond the relational structures and show that pre-training the node attributes produces the best node attributes for inductive link prediction.

[Reviewer] Reproducibility must be improved. Most of the details are omitted. For example, what are the characteristics of the MLP used in the paper? It is impossible to figure out if models are actually overfitted or if the process was correct.

[Response] Since we use a simple three-layered MLP for all the experiments, the chances of overfitting are low. We will add more details in the revised write-up of this work.

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We will incorporate them in the revised write-up of this work.

Adding our responses below:

[Reviewer] Weakness

[Response] (1) Our point is that graphs are generated by processes. In order to do inductive link prediction, you need to model the graph generation process. The current trend in ML is to increase the significance of the generated graph topology in learning. However, this prevents generalization in the inductive setting. (2) The node attributes commonly used and provided by the benchmark datasets aren’t informative enough for meaningful inductive link prediction, an issue that we resolve via unsupervised pre-training.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Proposes three datasets for inductive link prediction in graphs (based on OBG), compares vertex clusterings obtained by pre-trained node features on these graphs, and gives some results on the performance of selected models on the raw graphs and the graph + pretrained features.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I have a hard time spelling out strengths for this paper, unfortunately. 

W1. Benchmark tasks not convincing. The three tasks proposed by the paper are obtained by randomly splitting existing OGB datasets into train/validation/test nodes. While such an approach may be suitable for evaluating semi-inductive link prediction, it's not suitable for inductive link prediction. In fact, the so-obtained graphs are highly artificial, as the large number of ignored links between validation/test and train shown in the paper already suggests. (I say all this even though prior work also did such splits; I find them equally unconvincing.)

W2. Contribution unclear. The points made by this paper are already well-understood. Namely: (i) inductive is harder than transductive and (ii) external node features are useful. I did not gain any new insight from this paper. The paper makes an additional point about the clustering quality for various node features, but the relevance or potential insight of this approach remains unclear. In fact, feature selection should be a part of the model selection process anyway and it is clear that external features help above things such as random features (useless) or node2vec features (topology already exploited by GNN).

W3. Experimental study unclear. The paper presents some numbers, but is silent about the experimental setup so that these numbers cannot be interpreted. Moreover, on some tables, it's not clear which datasets or which model actually has been used.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The objectives of this paper are largely unclear. Quality and novelty are low. Reproducibility is unclear.
content.summary_of_the_review: Objective, contributions, take-aways, and experimental study are unclear.

content.title: Response to the reviewer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We will incorporate them in the revised write-up of this work.

Adding our responses below:

[Reviewer] Weakness 1

[Response] The understanding is absolutely correct in the case of random edge split. The majority of the edges are lost in the train-validation-test split while creating the inductive setting using a random edge split. Although random edge split is suitable for the transductive and the semi-inductive scenarios, it fails in an inductive test setting. This is the reason we use random node split for creating the train, the validation, and the test datasets for the inductive scenario. Random node split reduces the edges lost and provides a meaningful split for the inductive tests. 

[Reviewer] Weakness 2

[Response] The majority of the benchmark datasets deal with transductive link prediction which can be handled by simple models like the configuration model and does not require complex neural network architectures. The true potential of machine learning models is exploited in the inductive scenario. The major takeaway of the work is how to select the node attributes for improving the inductive test performance. We show that the node attributes that are often provided by the benchmark datasets (in our case, OGB) are not suitable for inductive tests. We show that unsupervised pre-training of the node attributes, beyond the nodes present in the training graph, is necessary for a successful inductive prediction. Our proposed method of quantifying the information contained in the node attributes empirically validates why the pre-trained node attributes are more suitable for inductive tests.

[Reviewer] Weakness 3

[Response] In all our experiments we use MLPs with three dense layers. We will incorporate the details in the revised write-up of this work.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3515 by Reviewer KEYu

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper considers the problem of fully inductive link prediction in networks where nodes have attributes or features. Link prediction is usually evaluated in the transductive setting where the objective is to predict edges between existing nodes. This transductive evaluation can be conducted both for networks with and without node attributes. Link prediction has also recently been generalized to what the authors call a semi-inductive setting, where the objective is to predict edges between new nodes and existing nodes by using both the network topology and node attributes.

The authors consider instead a fully inductive link prediction setting, which they refer to as simply "inductive link prediction," where the objective is to predict edges only between new nodes. This can be done only using node attributes. They demonstrate that current evaluation platforms and methods are not well suited for inductive link prediction and propose an alternative evaluation approach. Furthermore, they demonstrate that current approaches for link prediction perform poorly in the inductive setting. Finally, they consider the empirical performance of several approaches for creating node embeddings for inductive link prediction.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The authors demonstrate some key weaknesses both in current link prediction algorithms and evaluation metrics by leaving out the fully inductive setting.
- The authors propose an approach to properly evaluate inductive link prediction using existing datasets in the Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) that are not set up for such evaluation.
- The empirical novelty is high--the fully inductive setting the authors consider has not been given very much attention.

Weaknesses:
- The proposed inductive link prediction evaluation method in Section 5.1 only evaluates using edges between new nodes. While this is effective at evaluating inductive link prediction by isolating it, it does not consider the greater link prediction problem as a whole. The objective should be to predict all new edges between all nodes, regardless of whether they are new or existing.
- The authors claim that existing benchmark data sets and train/test/validation (TTV) splits do not allow for evaluation in the fully inductive setting. Their proposed method allows for evaluation in this fully inductive setting, but does not consider whether this is a realistic evaluation setting. Perhaps the existing TTV splits are indeed unrealistic, but perhaps the random node splitting method proposed by the authors is also unrealistic. In the older link prediction literature, researchers often considered dynamic networks and trying to predict new edges that would form in the future. In this way, we don't have to worry about whether the data splitting procedure is biasing the results.
- Presentation of the paper is very scattered. When writing an evaluation-focused paper, it is even more important (compared to a new methods-based paper) to clearly organize your main points and come up with several "take home" messages for the reader. This paper falls short in the organization despite the individual sections being decently written.
- Predicting edges between new nodes, i.e., the fully inductive setting the authors consider, may be of less interest to the machine learning community interested in graphs. It is the combination of graph data and node attributes that the community seems most interested in. The fully inductive link prediction setting doesn't involve the graph at all! Thus, fully inductive link prediction could be handled by an entirely separate module, e.g. the multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) that the authors consider.

Questions:
1. The discussion in Appendix B.4 suggests that the random node split strategy you adopt for evaluation often results in disconnected graphs and suggests that affinity clustering could result in a better node partition. Why did you not use affinity clustering for your evaluation? How do you handle the issue of disconnected graphs with the random node split?
2. The second part of Section 5.3 is based on a hypothesis that node attribute clusters that have minimal overlap with clusters obtained from the graph topology using Node2Vec are better for evaluating inductive link prediction. I think I understand the reasoning here. However, the first part of Section 5.3 seems to be based on an underlying hypothesis that node attributes that form more separated clusters are better for inductive link prediction. I am not sure of the reasoning here. Can you explain why this might be the case?

Typos and minor issues:
- Section 3, first paragraph: DTI is not defined.
- Section 5.3.1: I would suggest adding that a lower Davies-Bouldin score indicates better cluster separation, for the benefit of readers who are not familiar with it.
- Paper exceeds the 9-page limit for main body text by 4 lines. This should be an easy fix.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity: Medium. Individual portions of the paper are well written, but the overall organization could use significant improvement.
- Quality: Medium. Claims are mostly supported by the evidence, but there are a few decisions that I don't understand (see my questions above).
- Novelty: High. The fully inductive setting considered by the authors has not been given much attention, and their empirical findings can motivate future design of link prediction algorithms to better address this setting.
- Reproducibility: Low. No code is provided, and detail is lacking. For an evaluation-focused paper like this, having lots of details in the appendix is very important. Minor changes to small details could potentially skew the results.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I have very mixed feelings about this paper. I really like the novelty and think that the empirical findings demonstrate a clear weakness in current link prediction algorithms. However, I also hold evaluation-focused papers to a higher standard than typical methods-focused papers. A paper proposing a new method or algorithm for link prediction that has some flaws is not a terrible thing for the community--we can ignore it. An evaluation paper with some flaws could be problematic for the community if we then adopt flawed findings or evaluation metrics.

I commend the authors for considering this problem. I would not recommend publication at this time. However, I would really like to see an improved version of this paper published at a top venue in the future, because a strong evaluation paper of this type could have significant impact to the machine learning on graphs research community.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.

content.title: Response to the reviewer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful review and constructive comments. We will incorporate them in the revised write-up of this work.

Adding our responses below:

[Reviewer] The empirical novelty is high--the fully inductive setting the authors consider has not been given very much attention.

[Response] We thank the reviewer for recognizing the importance of this problem and its understudied-ness. 

[Reviewer] Weakness 1

[Response] Link prediction in all three (transductive, semi-inductive, and inductive) settings is important. We show that the majority of existing link prediction papers are transductive (e.g., the datasets in the OGB benchmark) and simple algorithms like the configuration model can achieve comparable performances to the neural network-based approaches. The true power of neural networks is leveraged in the inductive link prediction scenario, where the graph topology cannot be leveraged in the form of shortcuts. Thus, our work focuses on the most difficult scenario in link prediction, where the true potential of the machine learning-based approaches can be utilized. 

[Reviewer] Weakness 2

[Response] This is an excellent suggestion. Given a graph, random edge splitting fails to create a TTV split for the inductive setting, which is resolved via random node split. The proposed dynamic split is good too, but possibly even harder due to the distributional shift.  Our splitting method can also easily be applied across all link prediction datasets.

[Reviewer] Weakness 3

[Response] Thank you for the constructive feedback. We will incorporate this in the revised write-up of this work.

[Reviewer] Weakness 4

[Response] You are absolutely correct that the graph topology does not need to be considered for inductive link prediction.  Part of the message of our paper is that although the graph topology may lead to better performance in some scenarios, it also may lead to shortcutting and restrict generalization in others. We do believe even an MLP may engage the graph topology since we are modeling the underlying graph generation process instead of modeling signal propagation over a graph

Questions

[Q1 Response] Random node split is simple, we can repeat it with different seeds, and it's not influenced by the graph structure.  It simply assumes new nodes join the graph independently. That said, affinity clustering would be another good thing to try.
Since we do not leverage the topology of the TTV graphs in making inductive link predictions, disconnectedness does not affect the inductive test performance. 

[Q2 Response] The ability of the node attributes in clustering similar nodes (in terms of the node attributes) is a measure of the information contained in the attributes. We show that pre-trained node attributes produce the best clustering of the nodes, hence they contain the most information beyond the graph topology and are the most suitable for inductive tests.  

Summary Of The Review

[Response] We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the novelty of our work and the empirical finding demonstrating a weakness in the current link prediction algorithms.
